catalog_locator: sec. 3.1, p. 63; sec. 4.7, pp. 180-181 and 184; sec. 4.10, p. 192; p. 237; p. 248. page numbers, checked against running headers.
catalog_quote: In Saxwe, there are three tonal heights which are the realization of a three-way underlying tonal contrast: /H, M, L/. Utterance-final /M/ and /L/ are both realized with the final downglide that is frequently seen on utterance-final /L/ in many African languages. [p. 63] ... The default tonal assignment for borrowed words is that the nucleus of a syllable that would normally bear primary stress in the original language is assigned H tone and the nuclei of all other syllables are assigned L tone. This is seen in the following examples. In all of these examples, primary stress (and therefore H tone) falls on a non-final syllable of the word. [pp. 180-181] ... When primary stress in the source language falls on the final syllable, the word in Saxwe is assigned a H tone associated to the TBU of the final syllable—following the same principle as with other borrowed words. In addition, it is assigned a floating M tone following this TBU. [p. 184] ... The study of these pronominal suffixes also provides the clearest evidence for the claim that the mora, rather than the syllable, is the TBU in Saxwe. ... tone is assigned to borrowed words with relation to stress in the language of origin, with stress being reinterpreted as H tone in Saxwe (section 4.7). [p. 192]

new_statements.second_reader_evidence: Opened (365 pdf pages, text; printed page = pdf page - 14, checked by headers). All three quoted fragments are present verbatim at the stated locators: p. 77 = printed p. 63, sec. 3.1 heading 'A three-way system: /H, M, L/', first sentence 'In Saxwe, there are three tonal heights which are the realization of a three-way underlying tonal contrast: /H, M, L/.'; pp. 194-195 = printed pp. 180-181, sec. 4.7 'Nouns borrowed from English': 'The default tonal assignment for borrowed words is that the nucleus of a syllable that would normally bear primary stress in the original language is assigned H tone and the nuclei of all other syllables are assigned L tone.' (sentence breaks across the page);…
new_statements.rule_in_words: Saxwe is a three-tone language (H, M, L underlying; mora is the tone-bearing unit; lexical tone on nouns and verbs plus grammatical tone, tonal spread, downstep and boundary tones). The 365-page tone monograph and the 2013 segmental phonology sketch contain no section on stress or accent and no claim that Saxwe has word stress; the only mention of stress is that English primary stress is reinterpreted as H tone when words are borrowed (other syllables L, or L/M), which implies tone rather than stress carries word-level prominence.
new_statements.exceptions: For loanwords: when source-language stress is word-final the Saxwe form has final H plus a floating M (p. 184, p. 237); some loans take M instead of L on unstressed syllables (p. 248, e.g. 'teacher' /tʃítʃā/ vs 'tailor' /télà/).
new_statements.domain_note: Word-level lexical tone on monomorphemic nouns (V.C(C)V) and verbs (C(C)V), with isolation forms carrying an utterance-final L% boundary; loanword rule is word-level.
new_statements.identity_note: Saxwe = Saxwɛgbe = Sahouè (ISO sxw, saxw1241), Glottolog: Gbe > Western Phla-Phera; Capo classes it in Phla-Phera, Kluge 2007 in Eastern Gbe. Beavon-Ham 2019 describes the variety of the Houeyogbe district (the [dṹtũ̀] subdivision; principal consultant from Adrome), and notes Lobogo/Bopa ([dàkplâ], incl. the lect called Gbokpa) subdivisions; Daxe and Se are the closest neighbouring varieties (Johnson 2011 treats them separately).

tone_statements.citation: Beavon-Ham, Virginia R. 2019. Tone in Saxwe. PhD dissertation, Universiteit Leiden (LOT Dissertation Series 543). Amsterdam: LOT.
tone_statements.quote: In Saxwe, there are three tonal heights which are the realization of a three-way underlying tonal contrast: /H, M, L/. Utterance-final /M/ and /L/ are both realized with the final downglide that is frequently seen on utterance-final /L/ in many African languages. … While there are only three underlying tones, these tones combine to form a fairly large number of surface tone patterns that can be realized on monomorphemic verbs or nouns. … In Saxwe, either H or L will spread onto a TBU that carries M, delinking the M.
tone_statements.locator: sec. 3.1 'A three-way system: /H, M, L/' and 3.2 'Tonal spread', pp. 63-64; TBU = mora stated sec. 4.6.1 p. 173 and 4.10 p. 192
tone_statements.summary: Three level tones H, M, L, contrastive on every mora (the mora is the TBU); H and L spread over M; automatic and non-automatic downstep of H, the latter from a floating M; word stress not discussed.

tone_statements.citation: Adjamonsi Codjo, Aurore; Godefroy Sossou & Virginia Beavon-Ham. 2014. Lire et écrire en saxwɛgbe: Guide pour ceux qui savent lire le français. 1ère édition. Cotonou: SIL Bénin et Wycliffe Bénin. 72 pp. (SIL Language & Culture Archives entry 84839; archive record lists Beavon-Ham first).
tone_statements.quote: Le saxwɛ, comme beaucoup de langues africaines, est une langue tonale. Cela veut dire que deux mots identiques par rapport aux consonnes et aux voyelles sont prononcés avec une mélodie différente qui leur donne un sens différent. Cela est le cas pour les mots saxwɛ omɔ « chemin » et omɔ « machine ». Dans la plupart des cas, ces différences tonales ne seront pas marquées. [...] Le pronom 1ère personne du pluriel (« nous ») et le pronom 2ème personne du pluriel (« vous ») ne diffèrent que par le ton. Pour les distinguer, on écrit un accent aïgu sur le pronom qui veut dire « nous ».
tone_statements.translation: Saxwe, like many African languages, is a tone language. This means that two words identical in their consonants and vowels are pronounced with a different melody that gives them a different meaning. This is the case for the Saxwe words omɔ 'path' and omɔ 'machine'. In most cases these tonal differences will not be marked. [...] The 1st person plural pronoun ('we') and the 2nd person plural pronoun ('you') differ only in tone. To distinguish them, an acute accent is written on the pronoun meaning 'we'.
tone_statements.locator: Leçon 1, 'Les tons', p. 7; Leçon 11 'Les pronoms', p. 41 (also Leçon 10 §3.1 'Les mots ká et ka', p. 37)

No section on stress/accent; phonology overview (sec. 1.4, pp. 6-16) never mentions stress. The only stress statements concern English loanwords: the syllable bearing primary stress in the source language gets H tone, other syllables L (pp. 180-181, 184), 'stress being reinterpreted as H tone in Saxwe' (p. 192), final-stressed loans get final H plus floating M (p. 237).

sources.locator: Leçon 1, 'Les tons', p. 7; Leçon 11 'Les pronoms', p. 41 (also Leçon 10 §3.1 'Les mots ká et ka', p. 37)
sources.note: First-hand orthography statement: Saxwe is a tone language (minimal pair omɔ 'chemin' vs omɔ 'machine' differing only in melody); in the practical orthography tonal differences are as a rule NOT written, with two conventional exceptions taught in the guide: acute accent on mí 'nous' (1PL) vs unmarked mi 'vous' (2PL), carried over to derived forms (míatɔn 'notre' vs miatɔn 'votre'), and acute on prohibitive ká vs unmarked ka (volitive/prospective) — i.e. tone distinguishes both lexical items and grammatical morphemes. No tone inventory or tone rules are given.
